{"tier": "statistical_data", "verdict": "not supported", "confidence": "high", "evidence": [{"claim_snippet": "93% of all human communication is nonverbal", "source_url": "https://www.scienceofpeople.com/body-language-percentage/", "note": "Explains the 93% figure is a widely repeated misinterpretation of Mehrabian's work, not a finding about 'all human communication'."}, {"claim_snippet": "Research by Albert Mehrabian showed", "source_url": "https://maestrogroup.co/communication-myth/", "note": "Quotes Mehrabian directly saying it is 'absurd to imply or suggest that the verbal portion of all communication constitutes only seven percent of the message.'"}, {"claim_snippet": "93% of all human communication is nonverbal", "source_url": "https://cornerstone.lib.mnsu.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1000&context=ctamj", "note": "Academic paper labels the generalized claim an 'urban legend,' noting most secondary sources repeat the formula 'without any qualification.'"}, {"claim_snippet": "93% of all human communication is nonverbal", "source_url": "https://mohit-chhabra.medium.com/93-of-our-communication-this-is-wrong-caf55b7f3015", "note": "States the equations were derived only from experiments on communicating feelings/attitudes (like-dislike), and are 'not applicable' otherwise, per Mehrabian's own website."}, {"claim_snippet": "93% of all human communication is nonverbal", "source_url": "https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Mehrabian", "note": "Identifies the finding as the '7%-38%-55% Rule,' specific to conveying feelings/attitudes, not all communication generally."}], "origin_trace": "Original source: Albert Mehrabian's late 1960s studies (published in journals, later summarized in his book 'Silent Messages'), which examined only cases where a speaker's single spoken word conflicted with their tone of voice/facial expression while conveying feelings or attitudes (like/dislike). Mehrabian derived the 7%-38%-55% split for words/tone/body language strictly in that narrow experimental context, not for communication broadly, and he has publicly stated the generalized claim misrepresents his work.", "reasoning": "Multiple secondary sources and academic commentary confirm the 93% figure originates from Mehrabian's narrow experiments on inconsistent emotional messages (feelings/attitudes), not 'all human communication' as the claim states. Mehrabian himself has explicitly rejected the broad generalization, calling it absurd, and scholars label the extended claim an 'urban legend.' Because the claim strips out the critical population and scope qualifiers (only applies to expressing feelings/attitudes with conflicting verbal/nonverbal cues) and asserts a universal rule the source data does not support, the claim is not supported by the original research."}

{"tier": "statistical_data", "verdict": "not supported", "confidence": "high", "evidence": [{"claim_snippet": "women speak about 20,000 words a day while men speak only about 7,000", "source_url": "https://languagelog.ldc.upenn.edu/nll/?p=4488", "note": "Linguist Mark Liberman traces this figure as an unsourced statistic that circulated in self-help books (notably Louann Brizendine's) with no verifiable original study behind it."}, {"claim_snippet": "20,000 words a day... 7,000 words a day", "source_url": "https://time.com/2992051/women-talk-more-study/", "note": "Reports that a University of Pennsylvania researcher tried to trace the 20,000/7,000 figures to their origin and could not find a credible study supporting them."}, {"claim_snippet": "women speak about 20,000... men only about 7,000", "source_url": "https://abcnews.com/amp/Technology/story?id=3348076&page=1", "note": "Describes the actual Mehl et al. 2007 Science study, which found women spoke 16,215 words/day and men 15,669 words/day, a non-significant difference, directly contradicting the 20,000/7,000 figures."}, {"claim_snippet": "A study found... 20,000... 7,000", "source_url": "https://www.researchgate.net/publication/6223260_Are_Women_Really_More_Talkative_Than_Men", "note": "Peer-reviewed Mehl et al. (2007) paper in Science concludes men and women do not differ significantly in daily word use, each speaking roughly 16,000 words per day."}, {"claim_snippet": "women speak... men speak only about 7,000", "source_url": "https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/women-talk-more-than-men/", "note": "Notes the 20,000/7,000 claim was widely popularized but scientifically unsubstantiated, and that rigorous research shows comparable talkativeness between genders."}], "origin_trace": "The earliest traceable point is Louann Brizendine's 2006 book 'The Female Brain,' which stated women use ~20,000 words/day vs. men's ~7,000; a University of Pennsylvania linguist (Mark Liberman, Language Log) investigated and found no genuine study behind these numbers, calling it an 'invented statistic.' The actual peer-reviewed research on this topic, Mehl et al. (2007, Science), found women spoke ~16,215 words/day and men ~15,669, a statistically non-significant difference.", "reasoning": "The specific 20,000 vs. 7,000 figures cannot be traced to any real study; linguists who investigated found the numbers appear to be fabricated or unsourced, originating from a popular science book rather than research. The one genuine, peer-reviewed study on daily word counts (Mehl et al. 2007) directly contradicts the claim, finding men and women speak nearly the same number of words per day with no statistically significant gender difference. Therefore the claim's figure is not merely reframed but factually wrong when compared to the best available evidence."}
